text: Last lesson we looked at how each platform structures a procedural block. Now let's zoom in on something more basic but just as different: how you declare a variable and put a value into it. The same three-line idea — a product name, a price, a ten percent markup — looks genuinely different on all four platforms, right down to the symbols you use.

T-SQL first, because it's home turf. Declare at product name, n varchar fifty, equals road bike. Declare at price, decimal ten two, equals five ninety-nine ninety-nine. Set at price equals at price times one point one. Every local variable in T-SQL carries that at sign — it's how you tell a variable apart from a column name at a glance, and declare can show up anywhere in the batch, not just at the top.

PL/SQL drops the at sign entirely and uses a totally different assignment symbol. Declare, product underscore name varchar2 fifty, colon equals road bike, price number ten two colon equals five ninety-nine ninety-nine, begin, price colon equals price times one point one, end. That colon-equals is PL/SQL's assignment operator — plain equals is reserved for comparison. And every variable has to be declared up in that declare section before begin; you can't introduce a new one partway through, the way T-SQL lets you.

Here's the genuine surprise: MySQL actually has two different kinds of variables, not one. Inside a stored routine's begin-end body, you declare price decimal ten two default five ninety-nine ninety-nine, and set price equals price times one point one — that's scoped to the block, like T-SQL's declare. But outside any block, you can also just write set at price colon equals five ninety-nine ninety-nine — a session variable, prefixed with at, that sticks around for your whole connection. These two are not interchangeable, and mixing them up is a real, common MySQL mistake.

PostgreSQL's PL slash p g s q l looks almost identical to Oracle here. Do dollar dollar, declare, price numeric ten two colon equals five ninety-nine ninety-nine, begin, price colon equals price times one point one, raise notice, end dollar dollar. No sigil, colon-equals assignment, a declare section before begin — this is one of the clearest places where PL slash pgsql's Oracle-inspired design shows through directly.

So: T-SQL's at sign and equals sign, PL/SQL's sigil-free colon-equals, MySQL's two separate variable worlds, and Postgres echoing Oracle almost exactly. Next lesson we move from declaring values to branching and looping on them — including a real surprise about which one of these four platforms has no native FOR loop at all. See you there.
